lessons.title: Der alte Brunnen: adjectives before a noun
lessons.goal: Describe places in town with an adjective before the noun: der alte Brunnen, die enge Gasse.

grammar.point: After sein an adjective has no ending: Der Brunnen ist alt. Before a noun it gets an ending. After der, die, das, dieser and welcher in the nominative the ending is always -e: der alte Brunnen, die enge Gasse, das historische Rathaus. Teuer, dunkel and hoch change their stem: teure, dunkle, hohe.
grammar.oneLine: Before a noun the adjective needs an ending: der alte Brunnen (after der, die, das it is -e).

mistake.why: An adjective in front of a noun needs an ending. After der, die and das in the nominative that ending is -e. After sein, though, the adjective stays without an ending: Der Brunnen ist alt.

terms.meaning: the small ending (here -e) that an adjective gets in front of a noun
the case of the subject: der alte Brunnen ist schön
der, die, das, dieser, welcher: the words that come before the adjective

cards.title: Before we start: from "Der Platz ist schön" to "der schöne Platz"
cards.body: Welcome to chapter 5, Leben in der Stadt. Mira, Ben, Leon and Anna get to know their town: a fountain, a bank, the Bürgeramt, directions and a polite request or two. You already describe things with sein: Der Brunnen ist alt. Today the adjective moves in front of the noun: der alte Brunnen.
steps: You already know: Der Brunnen ist alt, and the articles der, die, das.
New today: an adjective before a noun gets an ending, and after der, die or das the ending is -e.
By the end you can: describe places in town with a pair like der alte Brunnen or die enge Gasse.

examples.why: You know this already: after sein the adjective stays the same.
New today: alte stands before the noun and ends in -e.

cards.more: Think of a small hat. After sein the adjective walks around without a hat: alt. When it stands in front of the noun, it puts on a hat: alte. Today the hat is always the same one, -e, because the word before it is der, die or das. The chapter then grows step by step: new endings, then a bank visit, a trip to the office and, later, polite requests.

cards.title: Town words: Brunnen, Gasse, Ufer
cards.body: Chapter 5 is about life in a town. Six new words for today: der Brunnen (fountain), die Gasse (narrow street), das Ufer (river bank), die Fußgängerzone (pedestrian zone), der Fluss (river) and der Stadtteil (district). You already know Platz, Kirche and Turm. Learn every noun with its article.
cards.lead: The introduction showed der alte Brunnen. Before the adjective can move, you need the town words it will describe, each one with its article.

examples.de: Der Brunnen steht auf dem Platz.
examples.en: The fountain stands on the square.
The pedestrian zone is in the centre.

deeper.text: Many town words are compounds, and the last part decides the article. Fußgängerzone is Fußgänger plus die Zone, so it is die Fußgängerzone. Stadtteil is Stadt plus der Teil, so it is der Stadtteil. When you meet a long new noun, look at its last part first: that is where the article comes from.

example.de: Der Stadtteil ist groß.
example.en: The district is big.

cards.more: Picture a small map. In the middle is the square with the fountain (der Brunnen). Narrow lanes (die Gassen) run away from it. The river (der Fluss) flows past the town, and the bank (das Ufer) is the grass next to the water. A district (der Stadtteil) is a piece of the town, and a pedestrian zone (die Fußgängerzone) is the street where nobody drives.

cards.title: An adjective before a noun gets an ending
cards.body: After sein the adjective stays the same: Der Fluss ist breit. In front of the noun it needs an ending: der breite Fluss. From now on the ending has its own colour in the examples. You see three chips: the adjective (breit), the ending (e) and the noun.
cards.lead: You know the town words. Now the new idea: the adjective moves in front of the noun, and then it grows a small ending that gets its own colour.

examples.why: Before the noun: the ending -e has its own colour. Schön after sein has none.
Same idea: eng + e before the noun.

deeper.text: The ending does a job: it shows the noun type and the case. After der, die or das that job is already done by the article, so the ending can stay very simple. Later in the chapter other words do more work and the endings change. For now one rule is enough, and the colour helps you see it fast.

example.de: Das alte Ufer ist ruhig.
example.en: The old river bank is quiet.

cards.more: Ask one question: is the adjective after sein, or in front of a noun? After sein it stands alone: Der Fluss ist breit. In front of a noun it needs a hat, the ending: der breite Fluss. A common slip is to put the ending after sein, too: Der Fluss ist breite. That is wrong. Say Der Fluss ist breit.
steps: Step 1: look: is the adjective after sein or before a noun?
Step 2: after sein: no ending. Before a noun: add an ending.
Step 3: after der, die or das the ending is -e.

cards.title: Nominative after der, die, das: always -e
cards.body: When the subject has der, die or das, the adjective ends in -e: der alte Brunnen, die enge Gasse, das historische Rathaus. It is the same for masculine, feminine and neuter. Say the whole group as one block, article, adjective with -e, noun, and the ending will come by itself.
cards.lead: You saw that an adjective before a noun needs an ending. Now you learn which one: after der, die and das it is the same -e for all three genders.

examples.en: The historic town hall is big.

deeper.text: In chapter 4 you learned gute Laune and schlechte Laune as blocks. They have no article in front, and that needs another table, which comes later. You can already see the same -e at the end, so you are not far away. In this lesson the article always stands in front, and then the rule is easy: nominative means -e.

example.de: Die gute Laune hilft uns.
example.en: The good mood helps us.

cards.more: Imagine three boxes: masculine, feminine and neuter. Each box holds a different article (der, die, das), but the adjective always puts on the same hat, -e. So you do not have to think about gender here. Just look at the article, see der, die or das as subject, and add -e. The only change is the article itself.

cards.title: Dieser and welcher work like der, die, das
cards.body: Dieser (this) and welcher (which) change like der, die, das: dieser Brunnen, diese Gasse, dieses Ufer. After them the adjective also ends in -e in the nominative: dieser alte Brunnen, diese enge Gasse. A question with welcher has no adjective yet: Welcher Stadtteil ist lebendig?
cards.lead: The rule works for more than der, die and das. Here you meet dieser and welcher, which you know from A1, and you see that they pull the same -e behind them.

examples.de: Diese enge Gasse ist sehr ruhig.
examples.en: This narrow lane is very quiet.

deeper.text: Dieser, diese, dieses and welcher, welche, welches have the same endings as der, die, das, so they are called der-words. Notice that dieses and welches end in -es, but the adjective after them still has only -e. The rule is about the nominative: -e after any of these article words.

example.de: Dieses historische Rathaus ist sehr alt.
example.en: This historic town hall is very old.

cards.more: Treat dieser and welcher as the same team as der, die and das. They stand where the article stands, and the next word is the adjective with -e. If you can say der alte Brunnen, you can also say dieser alte Brunnen and welcher alte Brunnen. Nothing else changes in the nominative.
steps: Step 1: choose the article word: der, die, das, dieser or welcher.
Step 2: add the adjective with -e.
Step 3: add the noun.

cards.title: Spelling traps: teure, dunkle, hohe
cards.body: Three adjectives change their stem before the ending: teuer becomes teure, dunkel becomes dunkle, hoch becomes hohe. The e before the last letter drops (teuer, dunkel) and hoch loses its c. Two adjectives in a row both get the same ending: der alte, historische Brunnen.
cards.lead: You know the -e rule. Now the small traps: three common adjectives look different when the ending is added, and you need to learn them once.

examples.en: The expensive pedestrian zone is loud.

deeper.text: Why do they change? Teure and dunkle are easier to say than teuere and dunkele: two weak e sounds in a row are shortened. Hoch drops the c because hohe is how it sounds. After the ending is added you hear the same word, just smoother. Two adjectives each need the ending: der alte, historische Brunnen. Lila and rosa never take one.

example.de: Der alte historische Brunnen ist berühmt.
example.en: The old, historic fountain is famous.

cards.more: Say the stems out loud: teuer, so teur-, and then add e: teure. Dunkel, so dunkl-, plus e: dunkle. Hoch, so hoh-, plus e: hohe. Each time one little letter disappears. If you are unsure, say the group out loud, die dunkle Gasse, and listen: the correct form sounds smooth.

cards.title: Describe your town
cards.body: Now put it all together. Say the same idea in two ways: Die Stadtmitte ist lebendig. (after sein) and Die lebendige Stadtmitte gefällt mir. (before the noun). To give a number, use hat: Die Stadt hat 80.000 Einwohner. One short text about your town is a good first goal.
cards.lead: You can now make the ending, spell the three tricky stems and use dieser. This card lets you talk about a whole town in a few sentences, with and without the ending.

examples.en: I like the lively town centre.

deeper.text: Einwohner is the word for the people who live in a town. It is der Einwohner for a man and die Einwohnerin for a woman, and the plural die Einwohner has no ending. You say hat for the number: Die Stadt hat viele Einwohner. Think of Einwohner as the people who live in the town, not the ones who visit it.

example.de: Die Stadt hat viele Einwohner.
example.en: The town has many inhabitants.

cards.more: Describing a place is just two kinds of sentence. Sentence 1 states a fact: Der Stadtteil ist ruhig. Sentence 2 uses the same idea as a short label before a noun: Der ruhige Stadtteil gefällt Mira. Use sentence 1 when you say what something is like. Use sentence 2 when you want to say what you like or need. The ending only appears in sentence 2.

lessons.title: Mira braucht den neuen Kontoauszug: the accusative
lessons.goal: Say what you need at the bank, using adjectives in the accusative: den neuen Kontoauszug, die neue Bankkarte.

grammar.point: In the accusative after der, die, das, dieser and welcher only the masculine changes: der alte Schein becomes den alten Schein (-en). Feminine and neuter stay -e: die neue Bankkarte, das neue Girokonto. The same rule holds after für, ohne, durch and um.
grammar.oneLine: Masculine accusative: den neuen Kontoauszug (-en). Feminine and neuter stay -e.

mistake.why: Kontoauszug is masculine, and here it is the object. After den the adjective needs -en. The ending -e belongs to the nominative and to feminine and neuter groups.

terms.meaning: the case of the object: Mira braucht den neuen Kontoauszug
a noun with der: der Kontoauszug, der Schein
a verb whose first part moves to the end: Ich hebe Geld ab.

cards.title: Before we start: the masculine changes again
cards.body: Mira needs a bank statement for the new flat, so she goes to the bank. Today you learn to say what you need and what you want to do there. In A1 you learned that der becomes den when the noun is the object. The adjective joins in: den neuen Kontoauszug.
steps: You already know: der alte Brunnen (nominative -e) and Ich brauche den Kontoauszug (den for the object).
New today: after den the adjective ends in -en, and after die and das it stays -e.
By the end you can: say what you need, withdraw or transfer money and ask welchen Schein?

examples.why: You know this already: den marks the masculine object. Kontoauszug is new, but the pattern is old.

examples.en: The new bank statement is here.
I need the new bank statement.
examples.why: New today: after den the ending is -en.

cards.more: Remember the shadow idea: the masculine word wears an extra n when it is the object, den instead of der. The adjective gets the same n: neuen instead of neue. Feminine and neuter words stay the same as before. So only one gender changes, and the same trick works for diesen and welchen. This lesson uses the bank, so you learn the words for it, too.

cards.title: Bank words: Bankkarte, Geheimzahl, Schein
cards.body: Seven words for the bank: das Girokonto (an account for everyday money; you know Konto), die Bankkarte (bank card), die Geheimzahl (PIN), das Bargeld (cash), die Münze (coin), der Schein (banknote) and die Filiale (branch). Das Bargeld has no plural. Learn each noun with its article.
cards.lead: The introduction named the bank statement. Before the adjectives can change, you need the other words for the bank, each one with its article.

examples.de: Die Filiale ist in der Altstadt.
examples.en: The branch is in the old town.

deeper.text: The compound trick works again: the last part decides the article. Kontoauszug is Konto plus der Auszug, so it is der Kontoauszug. Girokonto is das Konto, so it is das Girokonto. Geheimzahl is geheim plus die Zahl, so it is die Geheimzahl. The first part tells you what kind of thing it is.

example.de: Das Girokonto ist neu.
example.en: The current account is new.

cards.more: Imagine a small bank counter. On it lies cash: der Schein (paper) and die Münze (metal). Next to them is the card in your hand, die Bankkarte, and the secret number in your head, die Geheimzahl. At the back of the room is the account that holds your money, das Girokonto. Die Filiale is the bank building on your street, one of the many branches.

cards.title: Accusative: den + adjective + -en
cards.body: In the nominative a masculine group is der neue Kontoauszug. In the accusative, when the group is the object, it is den neuen Kontoauszug. Two small changes: der becomes den, and the adjective ending -e becomes -en. Ask: whom or what does the subject need, see or lose? The answer is the accusative.
cards.lead: You know the bank words. Now the first new ending: how a masculine group changes when it is the object of the sentence.

examples.en: Mira needs the new bank statement.
Ben is looking for the old banknote.

deeper.text: Why -en? The article den already says: this is the accusative masculine. The adjective repeats the signal with its own n. Dieser and welcher work the same way: diesen and welchen.

example.de: Ben sucht diesen alten Schein.
example.en: Ben is looking for this old banknote.

cards.more: Think of the n as a small hook. The masculine article hooks an n in the accusative (der becomes den), and the adjective hooks an n, too (neue becomes neuen). Say the group as one block: den neuen Kontoauszug. A common slip is to change only the article and leave the adjective: den neue Kontoauszug. That is wrong. Say den neuen Kontoauszug.
steps: Step 1: find the verb and ask: whom or what? That is the object.
Step 2: is the noun masculine? Then der becomes den.
Step 3: the adjective gets -en: den neuen Kontoauszug.

cards.title: Feminine and neuter stay -e
cards.body: Only the masculine changes in the accusative. For feminine and neuter nouns the group looks the same as in the nominative: die neue Bankkarte stays die neue Bankkarte, and das neue Girokonto stays das neue Girokonto. So after die and das the ending is -e again. Die nächste Filiale means the nearest branch.
cards.lead: You know that the masculine gets -en. This card shows the two genders that do not change, so the whole accusative picture is complete.

examples.en: Ben loses the new bank card.
Mira needs the new current account.
She is looking for the nearest branch.

deeper.text: Why is the feminine and the neuter the same in both cases? In German, die and das look the same in the nominative and the accusative. That is true for the article, and the adjective follows it. So the -e spots are: nominative der, die, das, and accusative die, das. That is five spots, and everything else will be -en. Nächste is made like the other adjectives and means nearest; learn die nächste Filiale as a block now.

example.de: Ben sieht das hohe Hochhaus.
example.en: Ben sees the tall high-rise.

cards.more: Test: is the noun masculine? Look at the article. If it is der, you change it to den and add -en. If it is die or das, you change nothing. The group stays as it was. A common slip is to add -en to feminine words: die neuen Bankkarte. That is wrong. Only the masculine gets -en here. Say die neue Bankkarte.

cards.title: At the bank: abheben and überweisen
cards.body: Two useful verbs. Geld abheben means to withdraw money: er hebt Geld ab. Geld überweisen means to transfer money: er überweist Geld. Abheben is separable, so ab goes to the end: Ich hebe das Bargeld ab. Überweisen is not separable. Die Überweisung is the transfer. And mit Karte bezahlen means to pay by card.
cards.lead: You know how the accusative works. Now two bank verbs that take an object, so that you can build real bank sentences with an adjective in the group.

deeper.text: Abheben has a prefix ab that splits off, like anrufen: Ich hebe das Bargeld ab. In the Perfekt the ab stays inside the participle: Ben hat Geld abgehoben. Überweisen keeps its prefix, and the participle has no ge-: überwiesen. The stress tells you: AB-heben splits, über-WEI-sen does not.

example.de: Ben hat Geld abgehoben.
example.en: Ben has withdrawn money.

cards.more: Picture two things you do at a bank. With abheben you take money out of the machine: the machine gives you the cash, and the verb has a little word, ab, that jumps to the end. With überweisen you send money to someone: the verb stays in one piece. If you see ab at the end of a sentence, the verb is abheben.

cards.title: Accusative prepositions with an adjective
cards.body: Four prepositions from A1 always take the accusative: für, ohne, durch and um. The adjective after them follows the accusative rule: für den alten Schein (masculine, -en), ohne die neue Geheimzahl (feminine, -e), durch die enge Gasse (feminine, -e). Learn the preposition and the article as one block.
cards.lead: You know the verbs. Now you meet the accusative prepositions with adjectives, because they are everywhere: for the bank, without the card, through the lane.

examples.de: Ohne die neue Geheimzahl hebt Mira kein Geld ab.
examples.en: Without the new PIN, Mira does not withdraw any money.

examples.de: Leon zahlt für den teuren Kaffee.
examples.en: Leon pays for the expensive coffee.

examples.de: Ben geht durch die enge Gasse zur Bank.
examples.en: Ben goes through the narrow lane to the bank.

deeper.text: The rule is the same as before: the preposition makes the accusative, and the group follows it. For um you can say um den alten Brunnen, with den and -en for masculine. Notice that the spelling traps from lesson 1 still work: teuer becomes teur-, so you write den teuren Kaffee and die teure Bank.

example.de: Wir gehen um den alten Brunnen.
example.en: We walk around the old fountain.

cards.more: Read the preposition first, then look at the noun. Für, ohne, durch and um say accusative. If the noun is masculine, you need den and -en. If it is feminine or neuter, you need die or das and -e. For an easy memory, say this like a song: für den, durch die, ohne das, um den. Then add the adjective.

cards.title: Ask with welchen: short answers
cards.body: To ask which one, use the accusative of welcher: Welchen Schein brauchst du? (masculine), Welche Münze? (feminine), Welches Konto? (neuter). A short answer repeats the group with the adjective: Den großen Schein. Die kleine Münze. Das neue Konto. The question itself has no adjective, so it needs no ending.
cards.lead: You can now build accusative groups in a statement. Here you use them in a dialogue: a question with welch- and a short answer that carries the ending.

deeper.text: Short answers are very common in real conversations. You do not say the whole sentence again. You just repeat the article, the adjective and the noun, in the same case as the question. You can even drop the noun: Welchen Schein brauchst du? Den großen. The ending stays, because the group still has to show which one you mean.

example.de: Den großen.
example.en: The big one.
example.why: The noun can be dropped, but the ending stays.

cards.more: In a dialogue, the question and the answer have the same case. Welchen goes with den, welche with die, welches with das. First hear the question: the ending of welch- tells you the gender. Then answer with the matching article and adjective. If you hear welchen, think: den ... -en.

lessons.title: Auf dem Bürgeramt: dative and plural, the whole table
lessons.goal: Get through a visit to the Bürgeramt and complete the adjective table: dative -en, plural -en, -e in five spots.

grammar.point: After der, die, das, dieser and welcher the adjective ends in -e in five spots (nominative masculine, feminine, neuter; accusative feminine, neuter) and in -en everywhere else: in the dative (mit dem neuen Formular, mit der neuen Wartenummer), in the masculine accusative (den neuen Schalter) and in the plural (die neuen Formulare, mit den neuen Formularen).
grammar.oneLine: -e in five spots, -en everywhere else: dative always -en, plural always -en.

mistake.why: After mit the noun is in the dative, and in the dative the adjective always ends in -en. The ending -e belongs only to the five easy spots of the table.

terms.meaning: the case after prepositions like mit, bei, zu: mit dem neuen Formular
more than one thing: die neuen Formulare
the 12 boxes (three cases and four groups) that show the adjective ending

cards.title: Before we start: the easy rule for the rest
cards.body: Ben needs a new ID card, so he goes to the Bürgeramt, the town office for documents. Counters, forms and queue numbers wait for him. Today you finish the adjective table. The good news: after der, die, das the rest of the table is almost all one ending, -en, and you only have to remember five spots with -e.
steps: You already know: der alte Brunnen (-e), den alten Schein (masculine accusative -en) and mit dem Formular (dative, A1).
New today: in the dative and in the plural the adjective ends in -en, and the whole table fits in one rule.
By the end you can: say mit dem neuen Formular, die neuen Formulare and get through a visit to the Bürgeramt.

examples.why: You know this already: mit takes the dative, dem for masculine and neuter.

examples.en: Mira needs the new bank statement.

examples.de: Ben kommt mit dem neuen Formular.
examples.en: Ben comes with the new form.
examples.why: New today: after mit dem the adjective ends in -en.

cards.more: Imagine a table with twelve boxes: three cases and four groups (masculine, feminine, neuter, plural). Five boxes have the -e hat you already know. The other seven have -en. So the rule is: -e only in five easy spots, -en everywhere else. This lesson shows you the dative, then the plural, then the whole table, and then you go through a real visit with Ben.

cards.title: At the Bürgeramt: words and steps
cards.body: Eight words for the office: das Bürgeramt (the town office), der Schalter (counter), die Wartenummer (queue number), das Formular (form), der Antrag (application), der Personalausweis (ID card), die Unterschrift (signature) and die Gebühr (fee). The visit has steps: Wartenummer ziehen, warten, zum Schalter gehen, Formular ausfüllen, unterschreiben, Gebühr bezahlen.
cards.lead: The introduction promised a visit to the office. First you meet the words, and the steps of the visit in order, so that you know what happens at each counter.

examples.why: Eine Wartenummer ziehen: a block for taking a number.

deeper.text: The last-part trick helps again. Bürgeramt is Bürger plus das Amt, so it is das Bürgeramt. Personalausweis is Personal plus der Ausweis, so it is der Personalausweis. Wartenummer is warten plus die Nummer, so it is die Wartenummer. A queue number is a small paper with a number on it; you take one at the door.

example.de: Das Bürgeramt ist in der Altstadt.
example.en: The town office is in the old town.

cards.more: Picture the room. At the door is a machine: you pull a number, die Wartenummer. You wait on a chair. When your number shows on the screen, you go to a counter, der Schalter. There you put a paper on the table: das Formular. You sign it, die Unterschrift, and you pay the small amount, die Gebühr. At the end you get your document.
steps: Step 1: eine Wartenummer ziehen.
Step 2: warten, bis die Nummer kommt.
Step 3: zum Schalter gehen und das Formular ausfüllen.
Step 4: unterschreiben und die Gebühr bezahlen.

cards.title: The dative: always -en
cards.body: In the dative, the adjective after der, die, das always ends in -en. It is true for all three genders: mit dem neuen Formular (neuter), am richtigen Schalter (masculine, am = an dem) and mit der neuen Wartenummer (feminine). The dative comes after mit, bei, zu, von, nach, aus, and after in and an for a place.
cards.lead: You know the five -e spots in the nominative and accusative. Now the dative: one very simple rule, the same -en for every gender.

examples.de: Ben kommt mit dem neuen Formular.
examples.en: Ben comes with the new form.
Ben waits at the right counter.

examples.de: Ben geht mit der neuen Wartenummer zum Schalter.
examples.en: Ben goes to the counter with the new queue number.

deeper.text: The contractions zum, zur, am and im already contain the dative article, and the adjective after them has -en: zum neuen Schalter, im alten Bürgeramt. The dative article does the main job of showing the case, and the adjective follows with -en. You do not have to think about gender. After a dative signal, say -en and move on.

example.de: Mira hat einen Termin im alten Bürgeramt.
example.en: Mira has an appointment in the old town office.

cards.more: Test: does the preposition take the dative? Then the group after it ends in -en, whether it is masculine, feminine or neuter. A common slip is to use the nominative -e after the article: mit dem neue Formular. That is wrong. After mit dem the adjective needs -en. Say mit dem neuen Formular.

cards.title: The plural: always -en
cards.body: In the plural, the adjective after die or den always ends in -en, in every case: die neuen Formulare (nominative), die alten Anträge (accusative), mit den neuen Formularen (dative). In the dative plural the noun also gets an -n if it does not have one: Formulare becomes Formularen. Wartenummern already ends in -n.
cards.lead: You know the dative. The plural is just as simple: one ending, -en, in nominative, accusative and dative alike.

examples.de: Die neuen Formulare liegen am Schalter.
examples.en: The new forms are lying at the counter.
Ben is looking for the old applications.

examples.de: Die Frau am Schalter arbeitet mit den neuen Formularen.
examples.en: The woman at the counter works with the new forms.

deeper.text: Why is the plural so easy? The plural articles die and den do not show gender, so there is only one group. The adjective only has to show that there is more than one thing, and the ending -en does it. In the dative plural the noun takes -n too, as you learned in A1: den Formularen, den Wartenummern.

example.de: Ben braucht die langen Formulare.
example.en: Ben needs the long forms.

cards.more: Imagine a crowd of forms on the desk: more than one, so the plural. Whenever you see die or den in front of a plural, the adjective is -en. Nothing changes between the nominative, the accusative and the dative. A common slip is to forget the ending: die neue Formulare. That is wrong. Say die neuen Formulare.

cards.title: The whole table: -e in five spots
cards.body: Now you have the whole table, three cases times four groups. The -e hat appears in five spots: nominative masculine, feminine and neuter, and accusative feminine and neuter. Everywhere else the ending is -en: seven spots. It works the same after dieser and welcher. Say it as a rule and you can build any group.
cards.lead: You have learned each case on its own. This card puts everything into one picture, so that you can see the rule behind all twelve boxes.

examples.en: The new counter is on the left.
Ben is looking for the new counter.

examples.de: Anna wartet bei den neuen Schaltern.
examples.en: Anna waits at the new counters.

deeper.text: Dieser and welcher belong to the same family as der, die, das, so the adjective endings are the same after them. The dative of dieser is diesem for masculine and neuter and dieser for feminine; the adjective is -en either way: mit diesem neuen Formular. The -e spots are only the five easy ones, so learn them first.

example.de: Ben kommt mit diesem neuen Formular.
example.en: Ben comes with this new form.

cards.more: Say the rule like this: -e in five spots, -en everywhere else. The five spots are always the "nothing changes" spots: the nominative, plus the accusative of feminine and neuter. The change spots are masculine accusative, the dative, and the plural. If you are unsure, use -en: you will be right seven times out of twelve.

cards.title: Verbs at the office: ausfüllen and beantragen
cards.body: Two verbs for the visit. Ein Formular ausfüllen means to fill in a form: er füllt das Formular aus. Einen Personalausweis beantragen means to apply for an ID card: er beantragt ihn. Ausfüllen is separable, beantragen is not. You also know unterschreiben, to sign. Each one takes an accusative group with an ending.
cards.lead: You can build any group with an adjective. Now two verbs that take an object, so you can say what happens at the counter.

examples.de: Ben füllt das lange Formular aus.
examples.en: Ben fills in the long form.

examples.de: Ben hat den neuen Personalausweis beantragt.
examples.en: Ben has applied for the new ID card.

deeper.text: Ausfüllen has a prefix aus that splits off, like abheben: Ben füllt das Formular aus. In the Perfekt, ge- goes in the middle: ausgefüllt. Beantragen starts with be-, which does not split, and the participle has no ge-: beantragt. The participle is always at the end: Ben hat den langen Antrag ausgefüllt.

example.de: Ben hat den langen Antrag ausgefüllt.
example.en: Ben has filled in the long application.

cards.more: Tip: if you hear aus at the end of a sentence, the verb is ausfüllen. If the verb starts with be-, as in beantragen, it never splits. Look at the object: it is an accusative group, so the masculine gets -en (den neuen Personalausweis) and feminine and neuter get -e (das lange Formular).

cards.title: At the counter: richtig and falsch
cards.body: Richtig (right) and falsch (wrong) are the adjectives you hear most at an office. They take the normal endings: Sie sind am falschen Schalter. Wo ist der richtige Schalter? Gehen Sie bitte zum nächsten Schalter. You can use the polite Sie form from A1 and add bitte, and you already know Können Sie mir helfen?
cards.lead: You can talk about forms and ID cards. Here you use everything in a short dialogue: you are at the wrong counter and ask where to go.

examples.en: You are at the wrong counter.

examples.de: Gehen Sie bitte zum nächsten Schalter.
examples.en: Please go to the next counter.

deeper.text: Richtig and falsch also describe other things: die falsche Wartenummer, das richtige Formular. Use the table to choose the ending, the same way as for any adjective. A polite visitor says Können Sie mir bitte helfen? and a clerk says Einen Moment, bitte. You will meet more polite forms in lesson 4.

example.de: Das ist die falsche Wartenummer.
example.en: That is the wrong queue number.

cards.more: Dialogues have a rhythm. The clerk says what is wrong (am falschen Schalter), you ask where to go (der richtige Schalter), and the clerk tells you (zum nächsten Schalter). The three endings change because the case changes: dative -en, nominative -e, dative -en. Read the little dialogue aloud once, then cover it and say it again.

rows: Guten Tag. Ich möchte den neuen Personalausweis beantragen.
Gehen Sie bitte zum nächsten Schalter.

lessons.title: Könnten Sie mir helfen? Polite requests with könnte
lessons.goal: Make polite requests at the bank and the office with könnte, and answer them.

grammar.point: Könnte is the polite form of können: ich könnte, du könntest, er/sie/es könnte, wir könnten, ihr könntet, sie/Sie könnten. It stands in position 2 of a question and the infinitive goes to the end: Könnten Sie mir helfen? Konnte (without umlaut) is the past; könnte (with ö) is polite.
grammar.oneLine: Könnten Sie mir helfen? Polite verb first, infinitive last.

mistake.why: The polite form has an ö. Konnten (with o) is the past: Were you able to help me? As a request you need Könnten (with ö), and the infinitive helfen stays at the end.

terms.meaning: the polite and possible form of a verb: könnte = could
a question that asks for something in a friendly way: Könnten Sie …?
the basic form of the verb, here at the end: helfen, zeigen, geben

cards.title: Before we start: from "Können Sie …?" to "Könnten Sie …?"
cards.body: You already ask politely with Können Sie bitte …? and you know konnte, the past of können. Today you meet a third form, könnte. It sounds softer, and people use it at a bank, at an office and with strangers. Mira needs it now: she wants to open a Girokonto and must ask for help.
steps: You already know: Können Sie mir helfen? and Ich konnte nicht kommen.
New today: Könnten Sie mir helfen? The same question, one step more polite.
By the end you can: ask for help at the bank and the office, and answer a polite request.

examples.why: New: one umlaut, and the request sounds extra polite.

cards.more: Think of two kinds of "please". Können Sie …? is like saying "Can you …?" in English: fine, normal, polite. Könnten Sie …? is like "Could you …?" or "Would you mind …?". Nobody will be angry if you use Können, but with an official or a stranger the softer form makes a better first impression. Today you learn how it is built and when to use it.

cards.title: Two levels of polite: können and könnte
cards.body: Können Sie …? is already polite. Könnten Sie …? is one step softer, like "Could you …?" in English. Use it where you want to make a very good impression: at the bank, at an office, with strangers and with older people. With close friends, Kannst du …? is still fine.
cards.lead: The introduction showed the new form next to the old one. This card shows where each one belongs, so that you pick the right level of politeness in every situation.

examples.en: Can you help me? (to a friend)
Can you help me? (to a shop assistant)
Could you help me? (at the bank)

deeper.text: Konjunktiv II is the name of this soft form. In English you use "could" and "would" all the time. German uses it less often, but with könnte and a few other words it works the same way. You do not have to use it everywhere. A good rule: the more formal the place and the less you know the person, the more likely you want könnte.

example.de: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
example.en: Could you please help me?

cards.more: Imagine three people. Your friend Ben is in the kitchen: Kannst du mir helfen? A shop assistant is at the shelf: Können Sie mir helfen? The woman at the bank counter is behind a desk full of papers: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? The further the person is from your daily life, the more polite you can be. And you never lose anything by being too polite.

cards.title: The dotted chip: könnte is Konjunktiv II
cards.body: From now on the polite form has its own chip: orange with a dotted outline. It is the polite "could" form, called Konjunktiv II. It stands where können stood, in position 2 of a question. Like every modal verb, it sends the second verb, the infinitive, to the very end of the sentence.
cards.lead: You have seen Könnten Sie …? in plain verb colour. This card gives the polite form its own colour, so that you can find it in every sentence from now on, and shows where the other verb goes.

deeper.text: Why is it a different colour from the normal verb? Because it does a different job. A normal verb states a fact: Ich helfe dir. The dotted chip does not state a fact, it opens a polite possibility: Könnten Sie helfen? We are not saying you do; we are asking whether you could. That is exactly what a polite request is. The word order stays the same as with können.

example.de: Könnten Sie mir den Weg zeigen?
example.en: Could you show me the way?

cards.more: A common slip is to put the infinitive straight after Sie: Könnten Sie helfen mir? This is the same slip as with können. Remember the sandwich: the polite verb stands at the front, then everything else (Sie, mir, bitte), and the infinitive closes the sentence. Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? Say it as one melody: first word, middle, last word.
steps: Step 1: the polite verb in position 1 of the question: Könnten
Step 2: then the subject and the small words: Sie mir bitte
Step 3: the infinitive at the very end: helfen?

cards.title: All six forms: ich könnte, du könntest …
cards.body: Könnte comes from konnte, but the vowel has an umlaut: ö. The endings are the same as in the past: ich könnte, du könntest, er könnte, wir könnten, ihr könntet, sie könnten. Rule of thumb: ö is polite or possible, o is the past, and a is the present.
cards.lead: You know can (kann) and could in the past (konnte). This card puts all three side by side in one table, so you see that one letter changes the meaning of the whole sentence.

deeper.text: Notice that könnte has the same ending in ich and er/sie/es, just like konnte: there is no -t on the third person. The wir and sie/Sie forms are both könnten; the sentence tells you who is meant. For du and ihr the endings -st and -t are added: könntest, könntet.

example.de: Könntet ihr mir bitte helfen?
example.en: Could you (all) please help me?

cards.more: Learn the table like a story with three times. Present: Ich kann heute nicht. Past: Ich konnte gestern nicht. Polite or possible: Ich könnte morgen. In a request, the umlaut is what makes the sentence soft. If you hear a letter o in Konnten Sie mir helfen? it is a past question: Were you able to help me? With ö it is the polite request.

cards.title: To friends: Könntest du …? and Könntet ihr …?
cards.body: With friends you use du or ihr: Könntest du mir helfen? or Könntet ihr mir helfen? It is a little softer than Kannst du …? Often the thing you ask for is a person and a thing: mir (dative, to me) and the object. The infinitive still goes to the end: Könntest du mir die Bankkarte geben?
cards.lead: So far the polite request used Sie. This card takes the same pattern to friends, with du and ihr, and adds a thing you ask for, so that the whole sentence has several parts.

examples.de: Könntest du mir die Bankkarte geben?
examples.en: Could you give me the bank card?

deeper.text: A separable verb like anrufen stays in one piece at the end of the question, because it is an infinitive: Könntest du Leon anrufen? And with two objects, the person comes first, the thing second: mir die Bankkarte, not die Bankkarte mir. The person (dative) usually comes before the thing (accusative), as you know from A2 chapter 1.

example.de: Könntest du mir das Formular geben?
example.en: Could you give me the form?

cards.more: Mira stands at the machine and cannot find her card. She turns to Ben: Könntest du mir die Bankkarte geben? Ben smiles and answers: Natürlich! The sentence is short, it asks, it does not order, and it sounds friendly. Compare Gib mir die Bankkarte! That is an order, and between friends it can sound rude. With könntest the same wish is a request.

cards.title: At the bank and the office: requests you need
cards.body: At the bank and at the Bürgeramt you need a few sentences again and again. Ich möchte … says what you want. Könnten Sie … ? asks for something. Wer ist hier zuständig? asks who is responsible. You can learn them as blocks and only change the last words.
cards.lead: Now the form is ready for real life. This card gives you the typical sentences for the bank and the office, so that you can use könnte straight away on Mira and Ben's errands.

examples.en: I would like to open a current account.

examples.de: Könnten Sie mir die Unterlagen zeigen?
examples.en: Could you show me the documents?

deeper.text: Ich möchte is a polite wish, and it uses the same pattern as a modal verb: infinitive at the end. A good office conversation has two steps: first you say what you want (Ich möchte meinen Wohnsitz anmelden), then you ask for help with a detail (Könnten Sie mir bitte die Unterlagen zeigen?). Keep every sentence short and polite.

example.de: Sind Sie für die Beratung zuständig?
example.en: Are you responsible for the advice?

cards.more: Zuständig means "responsible for", the person or desk that deals with your matter. You will hear it often at offices: Dafür bin ich nicht zuständig, which means that another person must help you. So the question Wer ist hier zuständig? is very useful when you do not know which counter to go to. The Beratung is the desk where a person explains things to you.

rows: I would like to open a current account.
I would like to register my place of residence.

cards.title: Answering a polite request
cards.body: When someone asks you Könnten Sie …?, you answer with a short, friendly phrase: Ja, gern. Natürlich. Einen Moment, bitte. If you cannot help, say Leider nicht and add a hint: Gehen Sie bitte zum nächsten Schalter. The answer is as polite as the question.
cards.lead: A conversation has two sides. After learning how to ask, this card shows how to answer, because at the bank and the office you also hear polite requests and must react to them.

examples.de: Leider nicht. Gehen Sie bitte zum nächsten Schalter.
examples.en: Sorry, no. Please go to the next counter.

deeper.text: After the dative zum, the adjective ends in -en: zum nächsten Schalter. You learned that in lesson 3: the dative always has -en. Leider nicht alone sounds cold, so add the hint: Gehen Sie bitte zum nächsten Schalter. The woman at the counter does that in the dialogue below.

example.de: Natürlich. Wie heißen Sie?
example.en: Of course. What is your name?

cards.more: Here is a small dialogue. Mira: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? Ich möchte ein Girokonto eröffnen. Frau am Schalter: Natürlich. Einen Moment, bitte. Wohnen Sie schon lange hier? Mira: Nein, ich wohne seit einem Monat hier. Frau am Schalter: Gut. Dann brauche ich Ihre Unterlagen. Notice that nobody gives orders: it is all requests and friendly answers.

lessons.title: Ganz freundlich: polite intonation and softer requests
lessons.goal: Sound polite with softening words and a friendly tone, use könnte at the end of a clause and as an offer, and ask for information.

grammar.topic: Konjunktiv II: softer requests with könnte
grammar.point: Softening words (bitte, vielleicht, mal, kurz) stand after the subject and the pronoun, before the infinitive. In weil, wenn and dass clauses könnte goes to the very end, after the infinitive: …, wenn Sie mir helfen könnten. With ich or wir, könnte makes an offer: Ich könnte morgen wiederkommen. In a polite question the voice goes up at the end.
grammar.oneLine: Softening words in the middle; in a clause, könnte at the very end.

mistake.wrong: Ich hoffe, dass Sie könnten mir helfen.
mistake.right: Ich hoffe, dass Sie mir helfen könnten.
mistake.why: After dass the conjugated verb goes to the very end: first the infinitive helfen, then könnten.

terms.meaning: a small word that makes a request friendlier: bitte, vielleicht, mal, kurz
the melody of your voice: it goes up at the end of a polite question
a suggestion of something you could do: Ich könnte morgen wiederkommen.

cards.title: Before we start: it is not only the words, it is the tone
cards.body: In the last lesson you built Könnten Sie mir helfen? Today you make it sound truly friendly. In German, politeness lives in three places: small softening words like bitte and vielleicht, the melody of your voice, and a sentence that does not sound like an order. You will practise all three, and you will use könnte in longer sentences.
steps: You already know: Könnten Sie mir helfen? with the infinitive at the end.
New today: softening words, a friendly rising tone, and könnte at the end of a clause.
By the end you can: sound polite at an office, make an offer and ask for information.

examples.de: Könnten Sie mir vielleicht kurz helfen?
examples.en: Could you possibly help me for a moment?
examples.why: New: two small words make the request even softer.

cards.more: A request has a skeleton and a skin. The skeleton is the word order you know: polite verb, subject, the rest, infinitive. The skin is everything you add: bitte, vielleicht, mal, kurz and your voice. A learner who only knows the skeleton is understood. A learner who also has the skin sounds friendly, and at a counter that can make the whole visit easier.

cards.title: Softening words: bitte, vielleicht, mal, kurz
cards.body: Four small words make a request softer. Bitte means please, vielleicht means perhaps, mal is a friendly "just", and kurz means "for a moment". They stand after the subject and after a pronoun like mir, before the infinitive: Könntest du mir mal kurz helfen? You can combine two, but do not use all four at once.
cards.lead: The introduction showed a first softening word. This card names four of them and shows where they stand in the sentence, so that you can add them without breaking the word order.

examples.en: Could you just come for a moment?
Could you please wait a moment?

deeper.text: Mal is the most German of the four. It does not translate directly. It makes the sentence relaxed and casual, so it fits best between friends: Kannst du mal kommen? With an official you rather use bitte and vielleicht. Kurz is also useful as a promise: it will not take long. The softening words always sit in the middle, never after the infinitive.

example.de: Könntest du mir mal kurz helfen?
example.en: Could you just help me for a moment?

cards.more: A common slip is to put mal before du: Könntest mal du kommen? The softening word does not come first. After the polite verb, the subject always follows right away. Say it like a train: Könntest, then du, then the small words, then kommen. The same train works with Sie: Könnten Sie vielleicht kurz kommen?

cards.title: The melody of a polite question
cards.body: In a polite question your voice goes up at the end. Say Könnten Sie mir helfen? with a friendly rise on helfen. Say bitte softly and not too hard. If your voice goes down at the end, the same words sound like an order, even if every word is polite.
cards.lead: You now know the words. This card is about how they sound, because in German a polite sentence with a flat or falling voice can still sound unfriendly, and that is the most common mistake of learners.

examples.en: Could you help me? (voice goes up at the end)
Could you wait a moment, please? (voice goes up, bitte soft)
Could you repeat that? (voice goes up)

deeper.text: Why does the voice go up? A rising tone says: the answer is up to you. A falling tone says: this is settled. In a statement like Das ist ein Formular the voice falls, and that is right. In a request, however, you do not want to say that it is settled. Try it with a friend: say the same sentence twice, once rising and once falling, and listen to the difference.

example.de: Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?
example.en: Could you please help me? (soft bitte, voice goes up)

cards.more: You can practise anywhere. Say Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? aloud ten times, each time a little softer on bitte and a little higher on helfen. Record yourself if you like. A good sign is a small smile while you speak: it changes your voice without effort. A flat voice with a hard bitte sounds like a complaint, even if the grammar is perfect.
steps: Step 1: start at your normal level: Könnten Sie mir …
Step 2: say bitte softly, not hard.
Step 3: stress the last word a little: helfen.
Step 4: let the voice go up at the very end, like a question mark.

cards.title: Polite or rude: three levels
cards.body: There are three levels of asking. An order like Gib mir das Formular! sounds rude. A question with Kannst du or Können Sie is polite. A question with Könntest du or Könnten Sie is extra polite. At the end you can add Danke für Ihr Verständnis, which means "thank you for your understanding".
cards.lead: The tone, the softening words and the form könnte all work together. This card puts the three levels in one table, so that you can turn a rude sentence into a polite one yourself.

examples.de: Können Sie mir bitte das Formular geben?
examples.en: Can you please give me the form? (polite)

examples.de: Könnten Sie mir bitte das Formular geben?
examples.en: Could you please give me the form? (extra polite)

deeper.text: To change a rude order into a polite request, follow the same three moves each time. First, turn the order into a question with the polite verb in front. Second, add the person who asks (Sie or du) and bitte. Third, move the old command verb to the end as the infinitive. Gib mir das Formular! becomes Könnten Sie mir bitte das Formular geben? Nothing is lost, and the tone is completely different.

example.de: Danke für Ihr Verständnis.
example.en: Thank you for your understanding.

cards.more: Danke für Ihr Verständnis is a fixed phrase that officials and employees often say. You can also say it yourself when you must wait: the person understands that you are patient. It is a block: you do not need to change anything. The word Verständnis comes from verstehen and means "understanding", with no plural in daily life.

rows: Können Sie mir bitte das Formular geben?
Könnten Sie mir bitte das Formular geben?

cards.title: Könnte at the end of a clause
cards.body: Könnte also works inside weil, wenn and dass clauses. Like every conjugated verb in these clauses, it goes to the very end, after the infinitive: …, weil Sie mir vielleicht helfen könnten. You often use such a clause to explain why you ask: Ich frage, weil … Or to say what you hope: Ich hoffe, dass … könntest.
cards.lead: Until now könnte always stood at the front of a question. This card moves it to the end of a clause, using the verb-at-the-end rule you know from weil, wenn and dass, to give you longer and still polite sentences.

examples.de: Ich frage, weil Sie mir vielleicht helfen könnten.
examples.en: I am asking because you could perhaps help me.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, dass Sie mir eine Auskunft geben könnten.
examples.en: I hope that you could give me some information.

examples.de: Ich hoffe, dass du mir kurz helfen könntest.
examples.en: I hope that you could help me for a moment.

deeper.text: In the clause the order is the same as with können: conjunction, subject, the rest, the infinitive, and then the conjugated verb at the very end. With könnte this means that the dotted chip is the very last word before the full stop. Always ask yourself: which verb changes with the person? It goes to the end.

example.de: Ich hoffe, dass ihr mir helfen könntet.
example.en: I hope that you (all) could help me.

cards.more: A common slip is dass Sie könnten mir helfen. This is the order of a main sentence, but after dass the verb walks to the end. The two verbs end the clause side by side: infinitive first, könnten last. Compare: Können Sie mir helfen? (question) and …, wenn Sie mir helfen könnten. (clause). The same two words, in a different order.
steps: Step 1: the main clause first: Ich bin froh,
Step 2: wenn, the subject and the rest: wenn Sie mir eine Auskunft
Step 3: the infinitive: geben
Step 4: the polite verb at the very end: könnten.

cards.title: Ich könnte … an offer
cards.body: Könnte is also used for offers and possibilities. Ich könnte morgen wiederkommen means "I could come back tomorrow". This is no request, it is an offer: you suggest something you can do. Add eventuell (possibly) or ausnahmsweise (as an exception) to make it softer still.
cards.lead: So far könnte asked for help. This card turns it around: with ich or wir, it offers something, which is useful when you want to find a solution together with the person at the counter.

examples.en: We could pay in cash, as an exception.

examples.de: Ben könnte eventuell den Termin verlängern.
examples.en: Ben could possibly extend the appointment.

deeper.text: Notice the difference. Ich kann morgen kommen is a fact: it is possible, I will come. Ich könnte morgen kommen is a suggestion: it is possible, if that suits you. The person can say yes or no. Use the suggestion when the other person decides, such as at an office. Bar bezahlen means to pay in cash, and mit Karte means by card.

example.de: Wir könnten eventuell mit Karte bezahlen.
example.en: We could possibly pay by card.

cards.more: Imagine Mira is at the bank and has forgotten a paper. She does not demand anything. She says: Ich könnte morgen wiederkommen. The woman at the counter hears a polite offer and can answer: Ja, gern, or Leider nicht. The key is that könnte leaves the decision to the other person.

cards.title: Asking for information
cards.body: At offices you often need information. Ich hätte gern eine Auskunft is a fixed polite phrase: "I would like some information". Then you can ask Könnten Sie das bitte noch einmal erklären? If you do not understand something, nachfragen is better than guessing: Ich frage lieber noch einmal nach.
cards.lead: The last card brings everything together for a real situation: you need information and you may not understand everything. These blocks help you to stay polite and to ask again without any embarrassment.

examples.de: Könnten Sie das bitte noch einmal erklären?
examples.en: Could you please explain that once more?

examples.de: Ich frage lieber noch einmal nach.

deeper.text: Ich hätte gern is a block that you may use without understanding its grammar: it is simply the polite way to say "I would like". You know it from the café and the shop. Nachfragen is a separable verb: fragt nach, hat nachgefragt. Asking again is not rude in Germany: officials prefer one more question to a mistake on a form.

example.de: Mira fragt nach, weil sie die Gebühr nicht versteht.
example.en: Mira asks again because she does not understand the fee.

cards.more: Here is a short scene. Ben: Guten Tag, ich hätte gern eine Auskunft. Der Mitarbeiter: Gern. Was brauchen Sie? Ben: Ich möchte meinen Wohnsitz anmelden. Könnten Sie mir bitte die Unterlagen zeigen? Notice the polite path: a greeting, the fixed phrase, a short wish and a polite question. And if Ben does not understand the answer, he can say: Könnten Sie das bitte noch einmal erklären?

lessons.title: Durch den Park, über die Brücke: directions and the city app
lessons.goal: Ask for and give directions on foot with route prepositions and the right case, and talk about a city app.

grammar.topic: route prepositions with accusative and dative
grammar.point: Durch, über (across), entlang and um … herum take the accusative: durch den Park, über die Brücke, die Straße entlang, um den Platz herum. An … vorbei, gegenüber and bis zu take the dative: an der Kirche vorbei, gegenüber der Post, bis zum Brunnen. An adjective after the article follows the case: durch den kleinen Park, an der alten Kirche vorbei.
grammar.oneLine: durch, über, entlang, um … herum + accusative; an … vorbei, gegenüber, bis zu + dative.

mistake.wrong: Gehen Sie an die Kirche vorbei.
mistake.right: Gehen Sie an der Kirche vorbei.
mistake.why: An … vorbei is a fixed frame that takes the dative: an der Kirche vorbei.

terms.meaning: a small word that describes a way: durch, über, entlang, vorbei
a way that is longer than necessary: ein Umweg
the place where you are right now: der Standort

cards.title: Before we start: beyond "geradeaus und dann links"
cards.body: In A1 you learned to say Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann links. A real town also has parks, bridges and churches. Today you learn the little words that describe a route: through the park, over the bridge, past the church. You also meet the words of the city app.
steps: You already know: Gehen Sie geradeaus, links, rechts, bis zur Kreuzung.
New today: durch, über, entlang, um … herum, an … vorbei, gegenüber, and the words of a city app.
By the end you can: ask for a route, give a route with the right case, and talk about your location.

examples.de: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann links.
examples.en: Go straight on and then left.

examples.why: New: the route words come with a case.

cards.more: A route is like a story with places. First you walk to the park, then through it, then over a bridge, then past a church. Each of these steps has a small word: durch, über, an … vorbei. Each of them needs a case, and the good news is that you already know the cases. Today you only learn which small word goes with which case.

cards.title: Asking for the way, politely
cards.body: Start with a polite request: Entschuldigung, könnten Sie mir helfen? Then say what you are looking for: Ich suche die Post. Or ask with one block: Wie komme ich zur Post? Use zur with feminine places, and zum with masculine and neuter places: zum Bahnhof, zum Rathaus.
cards.lead: You can now ask politely with könnte. This card shows what to say next, so that your first sentence opens the conversation and your second one gets you an answer about the way.

examples.en: Excuse me, could you help me?
I am looking for the post office.
How do I get to the post office?

deeper.text: Wie komme ich zur Post? is a block: you can change only the last words. The little word zur is zu + der, as in A1: bis zur Ampel. With a masculine place you say zum: Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof? Be careful with the order: the verb komme is in position 2 after the question word, and ich follows it. The answer is a command with Sie, as you learned in A1.

example.de: Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?
example.en: How do I get to the station?

cards.more: Always begin with Entschuldigung. In German towns people are happy to help, but they like to be asked first, like at the bank. A short, polite opening is half of the answer. After the explanation, say Vielen Dank! and, if you did not understand everything, ask again: Könnten Sie das bitte noch einmal sagen? Slow and polite always works better than fast and sharp.

cards.title: Routes with the accusative: durch, über, entlang, um … herum
cards.body: Four route words take the accusative. Durch means through: durch den Park. Über means over, across: über die Brücke. Entlang means along, and it stands after the noun: die Straße entlang. Um … herum means around: um den Platz herum. The articles are the ones you know: den, die, das.
cards.lead: The introduction showed durch and über. This card puts four route words that all need the accusative in one place, so that you can learn the rule once and use it for every route in town.

examples.de: Gehen Sie um den Platz herum.

deeper.text: Only the masculine article changes in the accusative, as you know from lesson 2: der Park becomes den Park, but die Brücke and das Rathaus stay as they are. Entlang and herum are different from the others. Herum comes at the end, after the noun, and entlang stands after the noun as well. The two together with um make a frame around the noun: um den Platz herum.

example.de: Gehen Sie über die Brücke und dann links.
example.en: Go over the bridge and then left.

cards.more: Do not mix up über with the two-way preposition from A1. You know über as a two-way word: über dem Tisch (where?) and über den Tisch (where to?). When you cross something, as in a route, über always takes the accusative, because you move. A common slip is durch dem Park. Durch is always accusative: durch den Park, no matter what.

cards.title: Routes with the dative: an … vorbei, gegenüber, bis zu
cards.body: Three route words take the dative. An … vorbei means past: an der Kirche vorbei. Gegenüber means opposite: gegenüber der Post. Bis zu means up to: bis zur Ampel, bis zum Brunnen. The dative articles are dem, der, dem, so the feminine place says der, not die.
cards.lead: The last card was about movement through a place. This card is about movement past a place or up to a place, and about where something is opposite. These words need the dative, so you can practise the second case in the same context.

examples.de: Gehen Sie an der Kirche vorbei.
Das Café ist gegenüber der Post.
examples.en: The café is opposite the post office.
Go as far as the fountain.

deeper.text: An … vorbei frames the noun just like um … herum: the preposition an comes before, vorbei comes after. Gegenüber normally stands before the noun, but it can also come after: der Post gegenüber. Bis zu is a block you know from A1: bis zur Kreuzung. Zu always takes the dative, so you say zur (zu + der) and zum (zu + dem).

example.de: Gehen Sie bis zur Ampel.
example.en: Go as far as the traffic light.

cards.more: A common slip is an die Kirche vorbei. An is a two-way preposition, so learners think of the accusative because they are moving. But in an … vorbei the preposition is part of a fixed frame, and the frame always takes the dative: an der Kirche vorbei. Learn the whole frame as one piece, and you never have to think about the case.

rows: bis zur Ampel, bis zum Brunnen

cards.title: Route verbs: abbiegen and überqueren
cards.body: Two verbs are important on a route. Abbiegen means to turn and is separable: Biegen Sie an der Kreuzung links ab. Überqueren means to cross and is not separable: Überqueren Sie die Straße am Zebrastreifen. Both are commands with Sie, in the form you know from A1.
cards.lead: You know how to say where to go. This card adds the two verbs that you hear most often in directions, turning and crossing, so that you can give and understand a route with several steps.

examples.de: Biegen Sie an der Kreuzung links ab.
Überqueren Sie die Straße am Zebrastreifen.
examples.en: Cross the street at the zebra crossing.

examples.de: Der Fußgänger wartet an der Ampel.
examples.en: The pedestrian waits at the traffic light.

deeper.text: Abbiegen has the prefix ab, which goes to the end in a command: Biegen Sie ab. In the perfect it is ist abgebogen, because turning is a movement. Überqueren has no separable prefix: the stress is on -queren, and the perfect is hat überquert, without ge. A pedestrian, der Fußgänger, uses the Zebrastreifen, and a woman is die Fußgängerin.

example.de: Biegen Sie nach der Brücke rechts ab.
example.en: Turn right after the bridge.

cards.more: Here is a full route, step by step. Gehen Sie durch den Park. Dann überqueren Sie die Straße am Zebrastreifen. Biegen Sie links ab und gehen Sie bis zur Ampel. Each step is one short command. When you give directions, do not make long sentences: short steps, one thing at a time, and the other person can follow you.

cards.title: Route words and adjectives
cards.body: The route words can contain a place with an adjective. The ending follows the case that the preposition needs. After durch, accusative masculine: durch den kleinen Park. After an … vorbei, dative feminine: an der alten Kirche vorbei. After gegenüber, dative neuter: gegenüber dem neuen Bürgeramt.
cards.lead: You know the route words, and you know the adjective endings after der, die and das. This card puts the two together, so that the ending of the adjective shows the case of the route word.

examples.de: Gehen Sie durch den kleinen Park.
Gehen Sie an der alten Kirche vorbei.
Das Café ist gegenüber dem neuen Bürgeramt.
examples.en: The café is opposite the new Bürgeramt.

deeper.text: The rule from lessons 2 and 3 still works: after den, dem and der in the dative the ending is -en. After the accusative die or das it is -e. So for the accusative route words you get: durch den kleinen Park, but über die lange Brücke and um das neue Rathaus herum. After the dative words it is always -en.

example.de: Gehen Sie die lange Straße entlang.
example.en: Go along the long street.

cards.more: Imagine a walk through the old town. Gehen Sie durch die enge Gasse, über die alte Brücke und am neuen Rathaus vorbei. Read the endings aloud: enge (die, accusative, -e), alte (die, accusative, -e), neuen (dem, dative, -en). If you know the article, you know the ending. It is the same story as in lessons 2 and 3.

cards.title: The city app: Standort, Navi, Funktion
cards.body: The app shows your location, der Standort. The satnav, das Navi, shows the route. A function, die Funktion, is something the app can do. If you walked the wrong way, say: Ich habe mich verlaufen. A longer way is ein Umweg, a shorter way is eine Abkürzung.
cards.lead: The last card is about the digital side of directions. You learn the words that you need when you talk about the city app, and a few useful phrases for when something goes wrong on the way.

deeper.text: Sich verlaufen is a reflexive verb: ich verlaufe mich, and in the perfect ich habe mich verlaufen. It means that you lose your way on foot. For a car you say sich verfahren, but that is for later. A detour, ein Umweg, takes more time; a shortcut, eine Abkürzung, takes less time. Both words come from Weg, the way.

example.de: Das ist ein Umweg.
example.en: That is a detour.

cards.more: Here is a small scene. Anna stands at the station and calls Mira. Anna: Ich habe mich verlaufen. Die App zeigt meinen Standort, aber das ist ein Umweg. Mira: Geh bitte durch den Park. Das ist eine Abkürzung. Notice that Mira uses du, because they are friends. The route words stay the same: durch den Park is accusative, no matter who is speaking.

lessons.title: In die Stadt oder in der Stadt? Wo and wohin in town
lessons.goal: Say where you are and where you go in town, use adjective endings inside preposition phrases, compare a small town with a big city, and use phrases without an article.

grammar.topic: two-way prepositions in town; movement vs place verbs; prepositions without article
grammar.point: Movement verbs (gehen, fahren, laufen, kommen) answer wohin and take the accusative: in die Stadt, auf den Platz. Place verbs (sein, bleiben, warten, sich treffen) answer wo and take the dative: in der Stadt, auf dem Platz. An adjective inside the phrase shows the case with its ending. Some chunks have no article: zu Hause, nach Hause, zu Fuß, nach Wien.
grammar.oneLine: Wir gehen in die Altstadt. Wir sind in der Altstadt.

mistake.why: Gehen is a movement verb: it answers wohin, so the two-way preposition takes the accusative (die), not the dative (der).

terms.meaning: a verb that takes you from one place to another: gehen, fahren, laufen, kommen (question wohin?)
a verb that keeps you in one place: sein, bleiben, warten, sich treffen (question wo?)
a short fixed phrase you learn as one block, for example zu Fuß

cards.title: Before we start: the two-way prepositions leave the flat
cards.body: In A1 you moved things around the flat: Ich stelle die Lampe in die Ecke. In A2 chapter 1 you asked wo and wohin at school. Today the same prepositions go out into town: in die Altstadt, auf den Platz, am Fluss. You also learn short phrases with no article at all, like zu Fuß and nach Hause.
steps: You already know: the nine two-way prepositions, wo (dative) and wohin (accusative), and the adjective endings after der, die, das.
New today: movement verbs and place verbs in town, endings inside a preposition phrase, city words, and chunks like zu Fuß, nach Hause and bei Rot.
By the end you can: say where you are and where you go in town, and compare a small town with a big city.

examples.de: Ich stelle die Lampe in die Ecke.
examples.en: I put the lamp in the corner.
examples.why: You know this already: wohin in the flat.

examples.en: We are going into the old town.
We are in the old town.

cards.more: Think of the flat from A1 as a small model of the town. The lamp went into the corner (wohin, accusative) and then stood in the corner (wo, dative). In town it is exactly the same, only the places are bigger: you go into the old town, and then you are in the old town. Same prepositions, same two questions, same two cases.

cards.title: Gehen, fahren or sein? Movement verbs and place verbs
cards.body: Movement verbs (gehen, fahren, laufen, kommen) answer wohin? and take the accusative: in die Stadt, an den Fluss, auf den Platz. Place verbs (sein, bleiben, warten, sich treffen) answer wo? and take the dative: in der Stadt, am Fluss, auf dem Platz. The verb tells you the question.
cards.lead: In the flat you used stellen and stehen. In town the verbs change, but the idea stays: this card shows which verbs move you and which verbs keep you in one place.

examples.en: Ben is driving to the river.
Ben is waiting by the river.

examples.de: Wir treffen uns auf dem Platz.
examples.en: We are meeting in the square.

deeper.text: Be careful with kommen. With a two-way preposition it is a movement verb: Anna kommt in die Stadt. But aus and von are dative prepositions, not two-way ones, so they stay dative with every verb: Anna kommt aus der Stadt. Only in, an, auf and the other six two-way prepositions switch between the two cases.

example.de: Anna kommt aus der Stadt.
example.en: Anna is coming from the town.

cards.more: Ask yourself one question: does the person move from one place to another? Then it is wohin, and the article becomes accusative: den, die, das. Does the person stay in one place? Then it is wo, and the article becomes dative: dem, der, dem. Warten is a good test: when you wait, you do not move. So you wait am Fluss, never an den Fluss.

rows: in die Stadt, an den Fluss, auf den Platz
in der Stadt, am Fluss, auf dem Platz

cards.title: In den schönen Park or im schönen Park? The ending shows the case
cards.body: Put an adjective into the phrase and the ending joins in. Masculine: in den schönen Park (wohin) and im schönen Park (wo) both end in -en. Feminine shows the difference: auf die breite Straße (wohin, -e) but auf der breiten Straße (wo, -en). The five easy spots get -e, everything else -en.
cards.lead: You know the endings after der, die, das from lessons 1 to 3. Now they go inside a preposition phrase, and the ending helps you see the case.

examples.de: Mira geht in den schönen Park.
examples.en: Mira is going into the beautiful park.
Ben is waiting in the beautiful park.

examples.de: Das Auto steht auf der breiten Straße.
examples.en: The car is standing on the wide street.

deeper.text: Im and am hide the article inside them (in dem, an dem), but they are still dative, so the ending is -en: im alten Kino, am breiten Fluss. Ins hides das, the neuter accusative, so it is one of the easy spots with -e: ins alte Kino. Even when the article is short, the ending tells you the case.

example.de: Die Katze läuft in die enge Gasse.
example.en: The cat is running into the narrow lane.

cards.more: Remember the five easy spots: nominative der, die, das and accusative die, das. Only there the ending is -e. A preposition phrase is never nominative, so in town you only meet two of the easy spots: accusative die and das (in die breite Straße, ins alte Kino). Everything else, den, dem, der, im, am, takes -en. So most adjectives in a preposition phrase end in -en.

cards.title: Bürgersteig, Verkehr, Lärm: words for city life
cards.body: Der Bürgersteig is the path next to the street for people on foot. Der Stadtrand is the edge of the town, die Stadtmitte the middle. Die Grünfläche is a green space with grass. Der Verkehr means all the cars and buses, der Lärm is noise, die Luft is air.
cards.lead: You now know how to say where you are. This card gives you the words for what you find there: pavements, traffic, noise and fresh or dirty air.

examples.de: Am Stadtrand ist die Luft sauber.
examples.en: At the edge of town the air is clean.

examples.de: In der Stadtmitte gibt es viel Verkehr und Lärm.
examples.en: In the town centre there is a lot of traffic and noise.

examples.de: Die Kinder spielen auf der Grünfläche.
examples.en: The children are playing on the green space.

deeper.text: Watch the genders: der Stadtrand but die Stadtmitte, der Lärm but die Luft. Verkehr, Lärm and Luft are almost never plural, so you say viel Verkehr, viel Lärm. Am Stadtrand answers wo. If you go there, it turns into wohin with the accusative: Wir fahren an den Stadtrand. Same word, two cases.

example.de: Wir fahren an den Stadtrand.
example.en: We are driving to the edge of town.

cards.more: Picture a town from above. In the middle is die Stadtmitte with lots of cars (der Verkehr) and noise (der Lärm). Around the edge is der Stadtrand, with more green spaces (die Grünflächen) and cleaner air (die Luft). Between the street and the houses runs der Bürgersteig, where you walk. Five places, one picture.

rows: der Verkehr / der Lärm / die Luft

cards.title: Kleinstadt oder Großstadt? Comparing places
cards.body: Die Kleinstadt is a small town, die Großstadt a big city. Compare them with the comparative and als, as in chapter 2: In der Kleinstadt ist es ruhiger als in der Großstadt. Two new adjectives help: breit (wide) and schmutzig (dirty). Das Rad is a bike: Mit dem Rad fährt man schneller.
cards.lead: After the city words you can compare two kinds of places. This card puts the comparative from chapter 2 into town: quieter, wider, dirtier.

examples.de: In der Kleinstadt ist es ruhiger.
examples.en: In a small town it is quieter.

examples.de: In der Großstadt sind die Straßen breiter.
examples.en: In a big city the streets are wider.

examples.de: Mit dem Rad fährt man schneller.

deeper.text: After sein the comparative is one adjective with no ending: Der Bürgersteig ist schmutziger. You can also compare two places in one sentence with als and two preposition phrases. Both phrases answer wo, so both are dative: Am Stadtrand ist die Luft sauberer als in der Stadtmitte. The case of each phrase stays the same on both sides of als.

example.de: Am Stadtrand ist die Luft sauberer als in der Stadtmitte.
example.en: At the edge of town the air is cleaner than in the centre.

cards.more: Think of two pictures side by side. Left: a small town, quiet, clean, narrow streets. Right: a big city, loud, a bit dirty, wide streets. Now say the difference with -er and als: Die Kleinstadt ist ruhiger als die Großstadt. Die Großstadt ist lauter. You already know this from chapter 2; only the places are new.

cards.title: Zu Fuß, nach Hause, bei Rot: phrases without an article
cards.body: Some short phrases have no article. Learn them as blocks: zu Hause (at home), nach Hause (home, moving), zu Fuß (on foot), nach Wien and in Wien (cities have no article), auf Deutsch, mit Karte or bar bezahlen, bei Rot (at a red light), ab Montag (from Monday).
cards.lead: So far every phrase in town had der, die or das. Now come the exceptions: short, very common phrases where German uses no article at all.

examples.de: Ich gehe zu Fuß nach Hause.
Bei Rot warten wir an der Ampel.
examples.en: At a red light we wait at the traffic lights.

deeper.text: These chunks also follow wo and wohin. Zu Hause and in Wien answer wo: Ich bin zu Hause, Anna ist in Wien. Nach Hause and nach Wien answer wohin: Ich gehe nach Hause, Anna fährt nach Wien. Nach without an article works only for home, cities and most countries. For everything else take in, an or auf with an article.

example.de: Anna fährt ab Montag nach Wien.
example.en: From Monday Anna is going to Vienna.

cards.more: A very common mistake is: Ich fahre nach die Stadt. Nach never takes an article in this meaning. For die Stadt you need a two-way preposition: Ich fahre in die Stadt. Keep nach for nach Hause and city names: nach Wien, nach Berlin. And zu Hause is where you are, nach Hause is where you go. If you remember that pair, the rest follows.

cards.title: Leon fährt in die Stadt: everything together
cards.body: Follow Leon through town. Every step has a wo or a wohin: Leon fährt mit dem Rad in die Stadt (wohin). Bei Rot wartet er an der Ampel (wo). Er parkt das Rad auf dem Bürgersteig (wo). Dann geht er zu Fuß auf den lebendigen Platz (wohin, masculine accusative -en).
cards.lead: You have learned the verbs, the endings, the city words and the no-article chunks. This card puts all of them into one short trip through town.

examples.de: Leon fährt mit dem Rad in die Stadt.
examples.en: Leon rides his bike into town.

examples.de: Er parkt das Rad auf dem Bürgersteig.
examples.en: He parks the bike on the pavement.

examples.de: Dann geht er zu Fuß auf den lebendigen Platz.
examples.en: Then he walks onto the lively square.

deeper.text: Parken (to park) is a place verb for the thing you leave: the bike stays there, so auf dem Bürgersteig is dative. Gehen auf den Platz is movement, so it is accusative, and lebendig gets -en because den is not an easy spot. When you tell a trip, check each phrase: is the person moving there, or already there?

example.de: Auf dem lebendigen Platz trifft er Mira.
example.en: In the lively square he meets Mira.

cards.more: Read the trip like a film. Scene 1: Leon on the bike, moving into town, wohin. Scene 2: a red light, he stops, wo. Scene 3: he leaves the bike, it stays, wo. Scene 4: he walks onto the square, wohin. Scene 5: on the square he meets Mira, wo. Moving scenes take the accusative, still scenes take the dative.
steps: Leon fährt mit dem Rad in die Stadt. (wohin: accusative)
Bei Rot wartet er an der Ampel. (wo: dative)
Er parkt das Rad auf dem Bürgersteig. (wo: dative)
Er geht zu Fuß auf den lebendigen Platz. (wohin: accusative, -en)
Auf dem lebendigen Platz trifft er Mira. (wo: dative, -en)
